Themes

System UI appearance is replaceable product presentation.

A theme owns chrome geometry, colors, controls, menus, taskbar treatment and theme-specific icons. App packages, System policy and host protocols remain unchanged.

Headless contract

The shell renders semantic parts — a caption and its control cluster, a menu bar, a launcher, a task strip, popups, selections, push buttons — and asks the active theme for their paint. Placement is data too: the theme's chrome metrics say which side the controls sit on, whether the menu bar lives in the window or along the top of the screen, whether the task strip flows from the left or centers as a Dock, and which edge desktop icons hang from. The window manager hit-tests from the same metrics, so no theme is special-cased outside its own definition. The file manager's toolbar and places sidebar are such parts: the same back / forward / up buttons, address strip, search field and place rows work under every theme, drawn as the Explorer coolbar and folder well, the Luna task pane or the Tiger gel pills and sidebar.

Theme boundary

Theme changes preserve each application's client rectangle. Window outer geometry is reframed through the selected chrome metrics, including normal, maximized and restore geometry. Pointer hit testing, caret placement and compositor surface placement all consume the same active metrics.

Switching

Open Start → Settings (the logo menu on Aqua) and choose a theme. During development, Cmd + Shift + T cycles through the themes.

Classic 98. Hard bevels, compact 18px chrome and a 28px taskbar.

XP. Three-stop Luna gradients, 21px caption controls, shaped close button and a 30px taskbar.

Aqua. Gel traffic lights on the left, a 22px glossy caption that goes matte when unfocused, the menu bar hoisted to a screen bar with the launcher logo and clock, a translucent Dock, right-anchored desktop icons and a vector icon set.

Rendering contract

All three themes lower to PocketJS DrawList operations. XP's and Aqua's middle gradient stops use the framework's via-* utilities, which lower to existing gradient rectangles and triangles; Aqua's gel highlights are stacked translucent pill layers because the backend paints no radial gradients. No theme adds a backend opcode.
